findings.primitive: walk up a parent array from a vertex until the root, within n steps, then test that the root was reached
findings.report: mesh_trees_check walks up a parent array at lines 327-329. The walk starts at v and ends at root r or after n steps. Then it tests that it reached r. mesh_graph_climb already does this walk. mesh_link_map_check calls mesh_graph_climb at line 109 of the same file. Three more loops walk a parent array by hand. They are mesh_route_nodes line 61, mesh_solve line 815 and routing_tree_check line 2877 of nccl-mesh.c. Line 326 checks only the parent of v. The walk at line 328 can read a parent that no check has seen. mesh_graph_climb stops at a parent that names no vertex.
findings.form: mesh_graph_climb(parent, n, r, v, visit, consumer). The visit keeps the last vertex it meets. The consumer tests that vertex against r. mesh_trees_check, routing_tree_check and mesh_solve each pass their own parent array. mesh_solve's visit sets tree[at] and treel[at].

findings.primitive: walk up one root's in-tree stored as a table column, keep the path, then reverse it
findings.catalog: mesh_graph_climb (needs a stride operand or a root-major table)
findings.report: mesh_route_nodes walks up one root's in-tree at lines 61-67. The parent of at is map->next[at*N+to]. mesh_graph_climb does this walk over a parent array. This table keeps parents by vertex, so the array is a column with stride N. The loop also stores each vertex in path. Line 69 then reverses path in a second loop. Line 65 calls mesh_joins at every step. Three more loops walk a parent array by hand. They are mesh_trees_check line 328, mesh_solve line 815 and routing_tree_check line 2877 of nccl-mesh.c.
findings.form: mesh_graph_climb with a visit that writes path[step] = at. The header needs a stride operand, or the table is kept root-major so each root's parents are contiguous. A route read the other way is path read from the end. The link test stays with the consumer, which runs it over path afterward.

findings.primitive: Dijkstra shortest path from one root in dense form, with a two-part cost
other_sites: rdma/mesh-collective.c:216 mesh_routes (the hop-extend sum of line 183, written again)
findings.report: mesh_distances is Dijkstra's shortest-path loop in dense form. Lines 176-186 pick the nearest unfinished vertex and relax its neighbours. mesh-graph.h has no shortest-path function. mesh_solve repeats this loop at lines 798-810 with a double length. mesh_routes writes the hop-extend sum of line 183 again at line 216. The sum adds one hop and the hop's inverse bandwidth. design/rubrics.md line 433 names a Dijkstra in the collective solver as a C9 case. Each copy scans all vertices to find the nearest, so each costs N squared.
findings.form: mesh_graph_shortest(vertices, edges, end, context, source, cost_size, extend, less, cost, parent). extend(context, edge, side, from_cost, to_cost) builds a neighbour's cost. less(context, a, b) orders two costs. mesh_distances passes (hops, inverse bandwidth) costs. mesh_solve passes a double length. mesh_routes calls extend again to find each node's tight parents.

findings.primitive: lexicographic compare of a struct's two keys
findings.report: struct mesh_length holds hops and inverse. mesh_shorter compares hops first, then inverse. mesh_equal tests both fields. This is a lexicographic compare for one struct. Sixteen other comparators do the same for other structs. They sit in mesh-collective.c, mesh-routed.c, mesh-graph.c, mesh-sparse.c, nccl-mesh.c and metal-recording.m. Four loop over a key array: mesh_message_order, mesh_move_order, physical_order and endpoint_order.
findings.form: mesh_graph_lex(left, right, keys) compares two uint64 key arrays in order and returns -1, 0 or 1. mesh_shorter passes {hops, inverse}. mesh_equal tests for 0. Each qsort comparator fills two key arrays and calls it.

findings.primitive: test one vertex in a bit set (a bit a vertex, 64 a word, NULL means every vertex)
findings.report: mesh_member tests one vertex in a bit set. A NULL set means every vertex. rank_member at line 6191 of nccl-mesh.c is the same function under another name. Four more places write the test inline. They are writes_weigh line 2816, routing_tree_check line 2876, fold_basis_seed line 3155 and fold_basis_validate line 3175, all in nccl-mesh.c. mesh_member is static, so nccl-mesh.c cannot call it. The set half repeats too. comm_routes line 497, demands_of lines 2708 and 2718 and backend.py line 278 set a bit by hand. mesh-graph.h has no bit set function.
findings.form: Two inline functions, mesh_set_has(set, v) and mesh_set_add(set, v), in mesh-plan.h, which both files include. A NULL set means every vertex in has. mesh_member, rank_member and the four inline tests become calls. Each consumer passes its own bit array.

findings.primitive: test whether any link joins an unordered pair of vertices, by scanning the link list
findings.catalog: none (mesh_graph_through ranks keys in a sorted array, but nothing sorts or groups edges)
findings.report: mesh_joins asks whether any link joins u and x either way. Lines 21-22 scan every link for that pair. Nine other places write the same either-way pair test. In mesh-collective.c they are mesh_parallel line 31, mesh_map_members lines 236 and 264 and mesh_solve_links lines 749 and 753. mesh_write_routes_compose in mesh-fabric.c holds two, at lines 285 and 302. mesh_transfer_order in mesh-routed.c has one at line 215. path_hop_split in nccl-mesh.c has one at line 2787. mesh-graph.h has no pair lookup. mesh_link_map_check calls mesh_joins N times N at line 91. Each call scans all links.
findings.form: mesh_graph_group(count, key, context, order, first). It sorts item numbers by key(context, i) into order[] and lists each run of equal keys as [first[g], first[g+1]). Links and cables pass key = (lower end, higher end). mesh_joins asks for a non-empty run. One sort replaces every scan.

findings.primitive: count and sum the links that join an unordered pair (group by pair, sum bandwidth)
findings.report: mesh_parallel counts and sums the links that join u and x. Lines 30-34 scan every link for that pair. This is a group-by-key sum with the pair as key. path_hop_split in nccl-mesh.c line 2787 sums cable bandwidth the same way. mesh_routes reaches this scan through mesh_hop_inverse at line 206, once per link. So each link rescans all links. Parallel links repeat the same sum. mesh-graph.h has no group-by function.
findings.form: mesh_graph_group, as for mesh_joins. mesh_parallel reads one run: its length is the count and the sum of weight(e) over it is the capacity. mesh_routes reads each run once.

findings.primitive: group links by unordered pair: count a pair's parallel links, then copy them, for every pair of a mesh
findings.report: mesh_map_members counts the parallel links of each mesh pair at lines 233-238. It scans all links for each pair. Lines 261-274 repeat the same pair loop and scan to copy the links. So one function writes the scan twice. Both scans repeat the pair test of mesh_joins. Line 285 then calls mesh_joins for every pair, which scans again. mesh_parallel and mesh_solve_links hold the same scan. mesh-graph.h has no group-by function.
findings.form: mesh_graph_group, as for mesh_joins. Lines 233-238 read each run's length. Lines 261-274 copy each run's edges. Neither scans the link list again.

findings.primitive: check that every edge names two different vertices below the vertex count
findings.report: mesh_routes checks at line 195 that every link names two different vertices below N. mesh_link_map_check writes the same loop at line 87. mesh_solve_links line 746 and mesh_fabric_check in mesh-fabric.c line 18 write it for links and cables. The loops differ only in field names and in what they do on a bad edge. mesh-graph.h has no edge check.
findings.form: mesh_graph_edges_bad(vertices, edges, end, context) returns the first bad edge number, or edges if none. Each consumer chooses to fail or to skip.

findings.primitive: exp and log built from exact operations so every node gets the same value
findings.report: mesh_exp and mesh_log rebuild exp and log from exact operations, at lines 294-310. They make every node compute the same value. No second copy exists in the repo. Both are static in mesh-collective.c. compile_form in nccl-mesh.c calls libm log at lines 424 and 437. Those values become log_weight, which mesh_exp reads later. Callers outside the file cannot reach mesh_log.
findings.form: mesh_exp and mesh_log as inline functions in mesh-plan.h. compile_form then calls mesh_log. They take no operands.

findings.primitive: find the trees of one root by scanning every tree for a matching root
findings.report: mesh_trees_check scans all trees for each node r at lines 317-321. It looks for a tree with root[t] equal to r. Four other places scan trees by root the same way. They are mesh_trees_heaviest line 339 and mesh_compile_sets line 469. In nccl-mesh.c they are root_carried line 402 and compile_form line 423. mesh_trees_pack writes trees grouped by root. mesh-graph.h has no group-by function.
findings.form: mesh_graph_group with key = root[t]. mesh_trees_check tests that every node has a run. mesh_trees_heaviest reads one run. The same call serves the other sites.

coverage.why: mesh_all is a one-line field sum. It has no loop.
Lines 21-22 scan the link list for a pair. Ten copies exist in the repo.
Lines 30-34 count and sum a pair's links. This is a group-by-key sum written by hand.
mesh_hop_inverse calls mesh_parallel once and divides. It has no loop of its own.
mesh_mark reads one field with a default.
Lines 61-67 walk up a parent table by hand. Line 69 reverses the path by hand.
mesh_route_path calls mesh_routes and mesh_route_nodes. It builds the whole N by N table to read one route.
It calls mesh_graph_cycle_length at line 106 and mesh_graph_climb at line 109. Line 87 holds the edge range scan listed under mesh_routes.
mesh_link_end is the edge-end operand that mesh_graph_reach takes.
The graph branch calls mesh_graph_reach at line 135. The table branch calls mesh_route_nodes for each pair.
mesh_member is a bit set test. Five more copies sit in nccl-mesh.c.
mesh_link_between calls mesh_joins or mesh_route_nodes. Line 154 is a one-line scan for a node on the path.
mesh_hash is the only splitmix finalizer in the repo. The FNV hashes at mesh-link.c lines 649-653 and 1977 are other algorithms.
mesh_shorter is a two-key lexicographic compare. Sixteen other comparators do the same.
mesh_equal is the equality half of the same two-key compare.
Lines 176-186 are a dense Dijkstra. mesh_solve holds a second one at lines 798-810.
Line 195 repeats the edge range scan. Line 216 repeats the hop-extend sum of mesh_distances.
Lines 233-238 and 261-274 scan the link list for each pair, twice. Both repeat the pair test of mesh_joins.
mesh_exp is a hand-built exp. It is the only one in the repo, and it is static.
mesh_log is a hand-built log. nccl-mesh.c calls libm log at lines 424 and 437 instead.
Lines 327-329 are a hand-written parent walk. Lines 317-321 scan trees by root.

findings.primitive: compare two records by a list of integer keys, first difference decides
other_sites: plus about 20 more qsort comparators in rdma/ (nccl-mesh.c, metal-recording.m, mesh-sparse.c, mesh-dataflow.c, mesh-tensor-layout.m, nccl-mesh-metal.m)
findings.report: mesh_message_order builds two key arrays of five words. It loops until the first key differs. Then it returns -1 or 1. mesh_move_order, mesh_packed_heavier and mesh-routed.c endpoint_order do the same. I count 33 qsort comparators in rdma/. Four of them use this exact key array loop. The catalog has no comparator or sort helper. Each consumer writes its own order and struct cast. This is the lower pole of C9.
findings.form: One header function that sorts records by a key list. A consumer passes a key function that fills a word array for one record, and the key count. The header owns the loop, the cast and the -1 or 1 rule.

findings.primitive: compare two records by a list of integer keys, first difference decides
findings.report: mesh_move_order builds two key arrays of six words and loops to the first difference. It is the same loop as mesh_message_order at line 374, with one more key. The pair sits side by side, three lines apart. The catalog has no comparator. Each ordered struct gets its own copy of the loop.
findings.form: The same sort-by-keys header function as for mesh_message_order. This consumer passes six keys: rank, round, receive, peer, key, part.

findings.primitive: compare two records by root ascending, then flow descending
findings.report: mesh_packed_heavier compares root first and then flow. The flow test is reversed, and it uses a double. It is used by one qsort at line 938. It is a third hand-written comparator in this file. The catalog has no comparator. This one is only a weak copy, because of the double and the reversed order.
findings.form: The same sort-by-keys header function. This consumer passes the root as a key and the negated flow as a second key, or a key function that returns a signed compare.

findings.primitive: sort records once, then scan runs and merge each record into the one before it
other_sites: rdma/mesh-routed.c:66-68 refine_pieces (run scan by rank after a sort)
findings.report: mesh_compile_sets sorts the messages at line 498. Then lines 500-506 scan them once. A message joins the one before it when from, to, round, buffers and step match and the parts touch. mesh-sparse.c does the same with intervals at lines 67-77. mesh-span-plan.h does it with plain values at lines 40-46. The catalog has no sort-then-merge function. Each site writes the sort, the scan and the keep index by hand.
findings.form: One header function that sorts records by a key function and then folds each run. The consumer passes a joins test for the last kept record and the next one, and a merge step. It returns the kept count.

findings.primitive: from records sorted by a key, find each key's first index (compressed row offsets)
other_sites: rdma/mesh-routed.c:282-283 dependency_order (count per rank, then prefix sum)
findings.catalog: mesh_graph_through (nearly: it takes uint64 arrays, and the ordered struct holds the rank inside a record)
findings.report: mesh_compile_sets sorts ordered at line 514. Lines 515-518 then walk the sorted rank field. They set first[r] to the count of moves below rank r. That is a rank query on a sorted list. mesh_graph_through answers the same query with a binary search. This code needs a uint64 key array first. dependency_order in mesh-routed.c builds the same offsets by counting and adding up.
findings.form: mesh_graph_through, or one row-offsets function beside it. The consumer passes the sorted rank keys and the node count, and gets first[] back.

findings.primitive: scan a parent table for a vertex's children and pick the least by height then number
other_sites: rdma/mesh-fold.h:24-27 mesh_fold_visit (scans every vertex for parent[child]==rank)
rdma/nccl-mesh.c:3182 fold_basis_validate (counts children of each rank)
findings.catalog: none (mesh_graph_tree_levels gives heights, but nothing lists children)
findings.report: mesh_first_child loops over all n vertices to find the children of w. It keeps the live ones and tests height, then number. Each call costs O(n). It is called at line 456 and line 489, inside loops over every node. So one tree costs O(n squared) here. mesh_fold_visit and fold_basis_validate also scan a whole parent table for children. The catalog has tree levels and ancestors but no children list. Heights come from the catalog; the child scan does not.
findings.form: A header function that visits a vertex's children over a parent table, or builds child rows once. The consumer passes a pick rule or a visit callback. mesh_first_child then becomes one call per vertex, not a scan per message.

findings.primitive: within the records that share a root, pick the greatest weight, lowest index on ties
other_sites: rdma/mesh-collective.c:469 mesh_compile_sets (collects trees of one root into parts)
rdma/mesh-collective.c:939-943 mesh_trees_pack (run scan of one root)
rdma/nccl-mesh.c:402 root_carried (any tree of root r)
rdma/nccl-mesh.c:423 (rank of a tree among its root's trees)
findings.report: mesh_trees_heaviest scans all trees for those with root r. It keeps the greatest log weight. It is called at lines 437 and 452, once per node pair. Each call rescans every tree. Five sites group trees by root with their own loop. The match is loose, since each site asks a different question of the group. I am not sure this is one primitive.
findings.form: A header function that gives each root's range of trees once. The consumer passes the tree roots and reads the group. Each question then runs over the group, not the whole list.

findings.primitive: cut n units into k pieces of near equal size, the first n mod k pieces one longer
other_sites: rdma/torch-mesh/torch_mesh/chain.py:59-61 _share (the same rule written as a relation)
findings.catalog: none (mesh_graph_cells cuts into fixed size cells, not equal pieces)
findings.report: mesh_cut_next finds where segment g ends in an even cut. It uses units divided by segments, plus the first remainder segments one longer. partition.py line 277 spells the same rule in one list line. chain.py _share spells it again as a text relation. The catalog cuts only fixed size cells. The rule is the same in all three; the code is not shared.
findings.form: One even-split function in the catalog, in C and in Python. The consumer passes the count, the piece count and an index. It gets the piece start and length. mesh_cut_next adds only the quantum and the size override.

findings.primitive: share units among weighted parts: floor of each share, then hand out the remainder
other_sites: rdma/mesh-fabric.c:110-138 mesh_write_ranges (floor of weight share, remainder to the largest remainder)
rdma/allocate.py:155-190 project (floor, then remainder by fraction)
findings.report: mesh_program_ranges floors each part's share of the units at lines 585-587. Then lines 588-597 hand out the remainder to the first parts. mesh_write_ranges in mesh-fabric.c does the same job with integers and gives the remainder to the largest fraction. allocate.py project does it in Python. The three differ in the remainder rule. They agree on the floor step and the sum check. Lines 579-581 also shift by the greatest log weight before exp. mesh_exp is called three times per part, at lines 581, 587 and 591. mesh_solve at line 789 shifts by a maximum the same way.
findings.form: One apportion function in the header. The consumer passes the units, a weight function per part and a remainder rule. It returns each part's count. mesh_program_ranges passes exp of the shifted log weight, and mesh_write_ranges passes the path weight.

findings.primitive: for each key, loop over all records and act on those that carry the key (group-by scan)
other_sites: rdma/mesh-collective.c:679-681 mesh_program_check_members (found and positive per segment)
rdma/mesh-collective.c:613 mesh_program_steps_cut (run scan of parts in one segment)
findings.report: mesh_program_ranges loops over all parts four times for each segment g. The loops sit at lines 580, 581, 586-587 and 589-590. Each one tests program->segment[p]==g. The cost is segments times parts, four times. mesh_program_check_members repeats the test at line 679. mesh_program_steps_cut scans a run at line 613. The catalog has no group-by on a key list. The match is loose, since the segment array is not promised to be sorted.
findings.form: A header function that gives each segment's parts as a range or row, built once from the segment array. The consumer passes the segment array and reads one row per segment.

findings.primitive: a set of integer intervals: add one with merging, and test whether one is covered
other_sites: rdma/nccl-mesh.c:5248-5272 spans_meet and spans_add (sorted disjoint ranges, merge on add)
findings.catalog: none (mesh_graph_span and mesh_graph_meets test overlap only; they do not union or test cover)
findings.report: mesh_defined_add keeps sorted disjoint ranges in a growing array. It finds where the new range starts and absorbs every range it touches. mesh_defined_has tests whether one range covers a query. nccl-mesh.c spans_add and spans_meet hold the same set. They are used for the same job, which is knowing which element ranges of a buffer are written. The two sets track the same fact in two files and can drift apart. The catalog's span functions answer overlap questions only.
findings.form: One interval set in the header: add, covers and meets. The set is the consumer's storage. mesh_program_check_members and nccl-mesh.c source relations both call it.

findings.primitive: grow an array by doubling, with an overflow check
findings.report: mesh_defined_add doubles its range array at lines 647-653. It checks for size overflow and keeps the old array on failure. This sits inside mesh_defined_add, which is itself a copy of an interval set. That makes it two layers deep. nccl-mesh.c has a shared grow function. The other four sites write the doubling out by hand, each with its own start size.
findings.form: One grow function in a shared header, as nccl-mesh.c grow is. The consumer passes the array pointer, its room, its count and the element size.

findings.primitive: free an array of structs that each own an array: free every inner array, then the outer array
findings.report: mesh_program_check_members allocates one mesh_defined array per rank at line 704. It frees each range, then the array, at lines 724-725. The set type has no free function, so the consumer writes the loop. The set is itself a copy, so this is two layers deep. I count nine loop-then-free sites in rdma/. Each pairs with its own allocation code. Most of them are plain frees, so the match is loose.
findings.form: A free function that comes with the interval set, and a make function for an array of sets. mesh_program_check_members then calls make and free once per rank.

coverage.why: It scans trees by root for the greatest weight. Other sites scan trees by root too. See the low confidence finding.
It calls mesh_graph_tree_levels at line 351 and mesh_graph_ancestors at line 353. Line 355 only marks a parent from a child.
It scans the whole parent table for children of w. The catalog has no child list.
It is a hand-written key array comparator. 33 such comparators exist in rdma/.
It is the same key array loop as mesh_message_order, with six keys.
It computes two room sizes from the tree count and node count. It has no loop.
Lines 496-506 sort and merge runs. Lines 514-518 build row offsets from sorted ranks. It calls mesh_member (line 145) and mesh_tree_shape. The rest is compile logic, not a primitive.
It forwards to mesh_compile_sets with global_segments set to 1.
It forwards to mesh_compile_sets with global_segments set to 0.
It takes one greatest-plus-one over the segment array. It is one short loop.
It writes the even split of n units with the remainder first. partition.py:277 and chain.py:59-61 write it again.
It is a running offset loop over mesh_cut_next. The copy is in mesh_cut_next.
It writes a weighted share with floor and remainder at lines 585-597. Its four segment scans at lines 580-590 are a group-by loop.
Line 613 scans a run of parts in one segment. This is the group-by scan found in mesh_program_ranges. The rest calls mesh_program_ranges.
It is the cover test of an interval set. nccl-mesh.c spans_meet is the same test.
It is an interval set add with merge, and it doubles its array by hand at lines 647-653.
Lines 704-725 loop over ranks, make a set array, and free it by hand. Line 679 is a group-by scan. The rest is validation and calls to mesh_cut, mesh_program_ranges and the set functions.
It is a two key comparator, root up and flow down. The catalog has no comparator.

findings.primitive: Dijkstra: shortest-path tree from one root, picking the nearest unsettled vertex each step
findings.report: mesh_solve runs Dijkstra by hand at lines 798-810. It picks the nearest unsettled vertex, then relaxes the edges at it. mesh_distances at lines 173-187 runs the same walk for mesh_routes. mesh-graph.h has no shortest-path function. The edge scan at lines 803-809 repeats the one in mesh_graph_reach. The copy sits inside the weights loop at lines 786-835. That makes it two layers deep.
findings.form: One mesh-graph.h function: shortest tree from a root over an edge list. Operands are end(e, side), the cost record size, a step(cost, e, side) function and a less(a, b) compare. mesh_distances passes an (hops, inverse) cost. mesh_solve passes a double sum of up and down lengths. Both read back parent and parent edge.

findings.primitive: walk up a parent table from each leaf, copying the vertices met into a tree
findings.report: mesh_solve climbs the up[] table at line 815. It copies each vertex it meets into tree[] and treel[]. mesh_graph_ancestors marks the same vertices up to the root. mesh_tree_shape at line 353 already calls it for this job. mesh_trees_check at line 328 climbs by hand too. So does routing_tree_check in nccl-mesh.c at lines 2879-2884. mesh_route_nodes at lines 61-67 does it on a next table. The copy in mesh_solve is inside the weights loop, two layers deep.
findings.form: Call mesh_graph_ancestors(up, n, root, leaf, marked) for each leaf. Then set tree[v] to up[v] where marked, else UINT32_MAX, and treel likewise. The two checkers pass mesh_graph_climb with a visit that tests each hop.

findings.primitive: find an equal tree row in a list of distinct rows, or add it, and count a hit
findings.report: mesh_solve looks for an equal tree at line 819. It scans every earlier tree and compares n words with memcmp. It adds a new tree at lines 820-825. It counts a hit at line 826. mesh_trees_pack does the same at lines 911-928. fold_basis_add in nccl-mesh.c does it at lines 3134-3148. Each copy scans the list in order. So the cost grows with the tree count, every demand, every round. The copy sits inside the weights loop, two layers deep.
findings.form: One find-or-add function over a table of distinct u32 rows. Operands are the table, the row width, a leading key and the row. It returns the slot. Each consumer adds its own weight to the slot: hits, flow or share.

findings.primitive: multiplicative-weights concurrent flow: lengths from loads, route every demand, add loads, repeat for T rounds
findings.report: mesh_solve is a multiplicative-weights flow solve at lines 786-835. Each round it sets edge lengths from loads, routes every demand, and adds loads. mesh_trees_pack has a second solve of this kind at lines 899-937. The two differ in the tree step and in the stop rule. mesh-graph.h has no solver. The round count is also written twice, at lines 765 and 784.
findings.form: One mesh-graph.h packing function. Operands are the edge capacities, the demands, eps, a stop rule, and a tree oracle called with the current lengths. mesh_solve passes a Dijkstra oracle. mesh_trees_pack passes mesh_graph_arborescence. It returns the distinct trees with their flows.

findings.primitive: Garg and Koenemann packing: grow edge lengths by (1 + eps x flow/capacity) until their weighted sum reaches 1
findings.report: mesh_trees_pack is a Garg and Koenemann packing solve at lines 899-937. It grows lengths until their weighted sum reaches 1. mesh_solve has the same family of loop at lines 786-835. Only the tree step uses the catalog, through mesh_graph_arborescence at line 904. The loop, the length update and the stop rule are written out here. The delta setup at line 899 uses mesh_exp and mesh_log.
findings.form: The same packing function as for mesh_solve. mesh_trees_pack passes mesh_graph_arborescence as its tree oracle, with the capacities and the stop rule D reaching 1.

findings.primitive: find an equal tree row in a list of distinct rows, or add it, and add flow
findings.report: mesh_trees_pack looks for an equal tree at lines 911-917. It compares each stored parent row with the new one. It grows the list by doubling at lines 918-923. It copies the new row at lines 924-927. It frees each row by hand at line 953. mesh_solve and fold_basis_add repeat this find-or-add. fold_basis_free at nccl-mesh.c line 3130 repeats the free loop. The copy sits inside the packing loop, two layers deep.
findings.form: The same find-or-add function as for mesh_solve. It owns the rows and frees them. mesh_trees_pack adds flow to the slot it returns.

findings.primitive: walk one compressed row of 32-bit words: through[e] to through[e+1] of crossing[]
findings.report: mesh_trees_pack walks the crossing lists by hand four times. The lines are 903, 906, 908-909 and 930-936. Each walk reads crossing[] from through[e] to through[e+1]. That is a compressed row of 32-bit words. mesh_graph_row visits such a row with a callback. Eleven more row loops sit outside this function. These four are inside the packing loop, two layers deep.

groups.report: Three functions list the four program arrays. program_free at nccl-mesh.c:263-265 frees segment, log_weight, first and move. program_copy at :353-364 allocates and copies the same four. program_compile at :369-381 callocs them and frees all four on failure. A new field in mesh_program needs edits in all three.

groups.catalog: none (mesh_graph_span and mesh_graph_meets test overlap only; they do not union or test cover)
groups.form: Add one interval set to a shared header: add, covers and meets. The set is the consumer's storage. mesh_program_check_members and the nccl-mesh.c source relations both call it. The doubling in add uses the shared grow.
groups.report: Three sites keep sorted disjoint ranges and merge on add. mesh_defined_add and mesh_defined_has sit at mesh-collective.c:630-658. spans_add and spans_meet sit at nccl-mesh.c:5248-5272. mesh-sparse.c:67-77 sorts intervals and merges touching ones. The first two track the same fact: which element ranges of a buffer are written. They can drift apart. The catalog's span functions answer overlap questions only.

groups.primitive: multiplicative-weights concurrent flow: lengths from loads, route every demand, add loads, repeat until a stop rule
groups.catalog: mesh_graph_arborescence (mesh-graph.h:51) serves only as mesh_trees_pack's tree step
groups.form: Add one packing function to mesh-graph.h. Operands are the edge capacities, the demands, eps, a stop rule and a tree oracle called with the current lengths. mesh_solve passes a Dijkstra oracle. mesh_trees_pack passes mesh_graph_arborescence. It returns the distinct trees with their flows, through the find-or-add function.
groups.report: Two solves share one loop family. mesh_solve at mesh-collective.c:786-835 sets edge lengths from loads, routes every demand and adds loads. mesh_trees_pack at :899-937 grows lengths until their weighted sum reaches 1. Only its tree step calls the catalog, through mesh_graph_arborescence at :904. The loop, the length update and the stop rule are written out in each. They differ in the tree step and the stop rule.

groups.primitive: round count T = floor(ln 2E / eps squared) + 1 of the multiplicative-weights solve
groups.form: Write the round count once, as rounds(edges, eps), beside the solver. mesh_solve_room and mesh_solve both call it. The eps guard stays with each caller.
groups.report: Two lines compute the round count. mesh_solve_room does it at mesh-collective.c:765. mesh_solve does it at :784. Both use ln(2E) over eps squared, plus 1. The guards differ. Line 764 replaces a bad eps with 1, and line 779 makes mesh_solve fail on a bad eps. mesh-plan.h says the trees made are at most the room. A change to one formula can break that.

merged.summary: Eight reports merged into 43 groups. The groups hold 340 sites, and each site is listed once per group. I dropped no finding. I read the code for the climb, Dijkstra, pair-scan, bit-set, row-walk, overlap and offset sites, and for the comparator definitions. Each is a hand loop. None is only a call to a catalog function. The real catalog calls stay out of the groups. They are mesh_graph_climb at mesh-collective.c:109, mesh_graph_ancestors at :353, mesh_graph_arborescence at :904, and the span, forward, row, cut_at and frontier calls in nccl-mesh.c at lines 2822, 4239, 4292, 4306, 4350, 4433 and 4506. Lines are those of ecdb4f2e, which I read with git show. The worktree is at a88732ac, two commits later, and only nccl-mesh.c differs. Its lines past 2780 have moved. For example, consumption_order_compare is at 3605 there. One reader cited six nccl-mesh.c comparators 40 to 48 lines off. I used the ecdb4f2e lines. At a88732ac, route_tree_counts and routing_prepare read trees by tree_first. That removes the scan at the old route_tree_counts site. solved_steps still scans. The catalog itself repeats primitives. mesh-graph.c holds three comparators, five offset builds, two binary searches and one sort-and-drop. mesh-graph.h has no compare, group, run, row-offset, lower-bound or shortest-path function. Order follows copies times deepest depth. Ties go to code that is hot in preparation. The LSTM plan comments name collective_steps, write_steps and the key scans as hot. Copies equals the sites listed. Some listed sites are homes or references, flagged in the site text: grow, mesh_log, mesh_packet_next, route_demand_sorting and the assignment.py dict. Low-confidence groups are the units, hop walk, edge range, laws, endpoint and bank groups. The comparator group is wide on purpose. One header function serves all 39 sites.
